To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the alpha activity in the human REM sleep can be divided into two variants: background alpha and REM-alpha bursts; (b) background alpha is modulated over occiparal regions by the presence or absence or rapid eye movements; and (c) the REM-alpha bursts, which are present in both tonic and phasical REM fragments, are independent of the presence and density of rapid eye movements.

the alpha activity during REM sleep has two variants, with different functional roles, which are the background alpha activity, which may be a correlate of visual dream contents, and the alpha bursts, independent of rapid eye movements that may facilitate the connection between dreaming brain and the environment.

(i) REM sleep alpha activity is characterized by the appearance of well defined bursts of activity not associated with the presence of rapid-eye-movements, (ii) these REM-alpha bursts are present in both tonic and phase-REM fragments and (iii) their topographic distribution and spectral power contribution are the same in both tonic and phase REM fragments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the alpha activity in REM sleep.
the analysis of the spectral characteristics of the EEG alpha activity recorded during the REM sleep.
the study of the alpha band in the sleep EEG, with the aim of determining its possible functional role.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the REM-alpha bursts, which are not associated with arousing processes, are a variant of alpha activity with a facilitatory role during REM sleep.
alpha activity during REM sleep is not a single phenomenon, but rather the result of two distinct alpha variants, each with a specific role in this brain state.
the REM-alpha activity is a specific variant of the EEG alpha activity with different functions than those of the background alpha activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the alpha activity during REM sleep is not a unitary phenomenon, but rather a complex one that includes two variants, one of them being the alpha activity that is modulated by the presence of eye movements, and the other, the REM-alpha bursts, which are independent of the presence/absence of REMs and which may be facilitating the connection of the dreaming brain with the external world.
alpha activity in human sleep is not only an electrophysio-logical marker of the cortical state but, also, an electrophysiology marker of the cognitive state.
the human REM sleep has a specific alpha activity which is independent of rapid eye movements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
alpha bursts in REM sleep are not a consequence of the presence of REMs.
the REM alpha bursts are a different variant from the REM-alpha background activity, with a different functional role.
REM-alpha bursts may be a useful tool in the investigation of the relationship between the dreaming brain, the external world and the sleep-wake cycle.
